Combined, this yields a maximum annual reproductive output of 6 eggs per year, a modest fecundity that is balanced by relatively high adult survival rates in a species that undertakes long-distance migrations between Fennoscandian breeding grounds and wintering areas in western Europe and Africa. The incubation duties are performed primarily by the female, who receives food deliveries from her mate during the 14-day incubation period. During egg formation, the female must accumulate sufficient calcium and protein reserves, a process that elevates her daily energy requirements considerably above the basal rate.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the brambling under natural conditions reaches approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], a remarkable longevity for a passerine of this body mass when measured in the same thermal context of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Evidence from long-term ringing studies in Scandinavia indicates that individuals returning to the same breeding territories year after year can achieve this age, though the median lifespan is considerably shorter due to high first-year mortality. The physiological mechanisms supporting such extended longevity in a 22.7 gram bird remain an active area of investigation, with hypotheses focusing on low oxidative stress levels and efficient cellular repair mechanisms. Comparative analyses with the closely related common chaffinch suggest that migratory behavior may select for enhanced physiological resilience.
